summary: This standards-track document defines a metadata format an OAuth 2.0 client can use to learn how to talk to an authorization server, including its endpoint locations and capabilities.

eli5.summary: Instead of guessing where the doors are, a program reads a sign that lists all the doors of a login service.

questions: what is oauth authorization server metadata
how does an oauth client discover endpoints
what is the oauth issuer identifier
subtitle: A JSON document at a well-known URL that tells an OAuth client where an authorization server's endpoints are.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 client needs to know an authorization server's endpoint locations and capabilities, and there was no standard way to learn them.
tldr.mechanism: The server publishes a JSON metadata document at a path built by inserting /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server into its issuer identifier URL, and the client fetches it with an HTTP GET.
tldr.outcome: Clients can configure themselves from one document, provided they check that the issuer value matches and use TLS certificate checks. The format generalizes OpenID Connect Discovery.

today: RFC 8414 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for OAuth 2.0 authorization server metadata.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8414 generalizes the metadata format of "OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0" so that it works for a wider set of OAuth 2.0 use cases while staying compatible with OpenID Connect Discovery. The RFC compares this to the way RFC 7591 generalized dynamic client registration.

The metadata is retrieved from a well-known location as a JSON document that declares the server's endpoint locations and capabilities. It can be served as plain, self-asserted JSON over HTTPS, or as signed metadata in a JSON Web Token, where the issuer vouches for the data.

How a client picks an authorization server is out of scope. The issuer identifier may be configured manually or discovered dynamically, for instance with WebFinger (RFC 7033).
sections.eli5: A login service has many doors, such as one for signing in and one for getting passes. This document is a standard map of those doors that a program can read on its own.

sections.title: The Metadata Values
sections.content:
The metadata is a JSON object of named values. The key ones are:

  • issuer (REQUIRED): the server's issuer identifier, an https URL with no query or fragment. It helps prevent authorization server mix-up attacks.
  • authorization_endpoint and token_endpoint: the endpoint URLs from RFC 6749. Each is REQUIRED unless the server does not support the grant types that use it.
  • jwks_uri: where the server's JSON Web Key Set is, which holds keys for validating its signatures. It MUST use https.
  • registration_endpoint: the Dynamic Client Registration endpoint.
  • response_types_supported (REQUIRED): the supported response_type values.
  • scopes_supported (RECOMMENDED): supported scope values.

Many more are optional. These include supported grant types, client authentication methods for the token, revocation and introspection endpoints, code_challenge_methods_supported for PKCE, service_documentation and ui_locales_supported. Defaults apply when some are omitted: response_modes_supported defaults to ["query", "fragment"], and grant_types_supported to ["authorization_code", "implicit"]. Additional parameters MAY also be used.
sections.eli5: The map has labelled entries, like "login door is here" and "ticket desk is there". Some entries are a must, and some are extras the service can add if it wants.

sections.title: Signed Metadata
sections.content: A server MAY also include a signed_metadata value: a JWT whose claims are metadata values about the server. It MUST be signed or MACed with JSON Web Signature and MUST contain an iss claim naming the party that vouches for the claims. A consumer MAY ignore it if it does not support the feature, but if it does support it, the signed values MUST take precedence over the matching plain JSON values. The signed_metadata value SHOULD NOT appear as a claim inside the JWT itself.
sections.eli5: The sign can carry a stamped copy as well. If you can check the stamp, you trust the stamped copy over the plain writing.

sections.title: Fetching and Validating the Document
sections.content:
A server that supports metadata MUST serve the JSON document at a path made by inserting a well-known URI string between the host and the path (if any) of its issuer identifier. The default string is /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, and the path MUST use https. An application may register and use its own suffix instead, and a server MAY publish at several locations.

The client sends an HTTP GET. For issuer https://example.com the request is for /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server on host example.com. For issuer https://example.com/issuer1 it is for /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/issuer1. Any terminating "/" on the issuer MUST be removed first. Paths allow several issuers per host.

A successful response MUST be 200 OK with content type application/json. Claims with zero elements MUST be omitted. Before using the data, the client checks that the returned issuer is identical to the issuer identifier used to build the URL. If not, the data MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: You find the sign by adding a fixed word to the service's web address. When you read it, check that the name on the sign matches the place you went to, or ignore the sign.

sections.title: Compatibility with OpenID Connect Discovery
sections.content:
Some names look OpenID-specific, namely /.well-known/openid-configuration, op_policy_uri and op_tos_uri, but the RFC says they refer to general OAuth 2.0 features. The URL transformation is equivalent to OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 when the issuer has no path. With a path, the two differ: OpenID Connect Discovery appends the well-known string (https://example.com/issuer1/.well-known/openid-configuration), while this RFC inserts it before the path (https://example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration/issuer1).

In legacy environments, a transition may require publishing at both locations. Applications should first try the location defined here and fall back to the OpenID Connect Discovery location only if that fails.
sections.eli5: An older sign-posting system put the sign in a slightly different place. New clients look in the new place first, and check the old place only if the new one is empty.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support TLS. The authorization server MUST support TLS version 1.2 (RFC 5246), and the client MUST perform a server certificate check per RFC 6125. Confidentiality protection MUST use a ciphersuite that gives confidentiality and integrity.

The main threat is impersonation. Attacks on the network or DNS could trick a client into using an attacker's keys and endpoints. Certificate checking against the issuer URL prevents this. An attacker could also publish a document claiming the real issuer but listing its own endpoints and keys, so the client MUST ensure the issuer URL used for the request exactly matches the issuer value returned.

The RFC also notes that publishing in a standard format makes it easier for attackers as well as clients, so the same defenses apply. Choosing the right protected resources for a server is out of scope, and a wrong choice might let an attacker act as a man-in-the-middle.
sections.eli5: Make sure you are really at the right place, and that the sign names that same place. Otherwise a trickster could post a fake map that leads you to their doors.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC creates the IANA "OAuth Authorization Server Metadata" registry. Values are registered on a Specification Required basis after a two-week review on the oauth-ext-review@ietf.org mailing list. It also registers the well-known URI suffix oauth-authorization-server.

It adds a rule for two existing registries, OAuth Access Token Types and OAuth Token Endpoint Authentication Methods. The Designated Experts must reject a value in one that already occurs in the other, so that introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, which accepts values from either, stays unambiguous.
sections.eli5: There is a public list of allowed entries for the map, so two services do not use the same word to mean different things.
